0.title: Amazing Grace from First to Last
0.overview:
The Bible ends with one word of blessing: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all. Amen. (Rev 22:21). After sixty-six books of creation, fall, law, prophets, gospel and promise, the last thing God says to his people is "grace." It is a fitting end, because grace runs through the whole story.

Grace is God's free, undeserved favour toward people who deserve the opposite. A simple way to remember it: mercy is God not giving us what we deserve; grace is God giving us what we do not deserve. We deserve judgment, and he gives forgiveness, adoption, the Holy Spirit, a new heart and eternal life. And he gives all of it freely, at his own cost, in Jesus Christ.

Grace is easy to say and hard to believe. Every human heart leans toward earning. We want to deserve God's favour, or at least to contribute something. That instinct produces two opposite errors. One is legalism, which tries to earn God's acceptance by keeping rules. The other is licence, which treats grace as permission to sin. Both misunderstand grace. Scripture shows a grace that saves without our works and then trains us to live for God.

This study follows the historic Reformed understanding of grace: that salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, and that God's saving grace does not merely make salvation possible but actually brings his people to faith and keeps them to the end. Where Christians differ on that, the main views are explained fairly.

Six units: (1) What Grace Is; (2) The God of All Grace in the Old Testament; (3) Saving Grace; (4) Grace Against Legalism and Licence; (5) Grace for Every Day; (6) Growing in Grace and Showing Grace. It belongs with the studies on the Holiness of God and the Fear of the Lord. Only those who see how holy God is will see how amazing his grace is.

1.title: What Grace Is
1.overview:
The clearest definition of grace in the Bible comes in a single sentence from Paul: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast (Eph 2:8-9). Every phrase excludes human contribution. Not your own doing. A gift. Not of works. No boasting.

Grace is the opposite of wages. Paul explains, Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due (Rom 4:4). If we could earn salvation, God would owe it to us. But grace is never owed. And Paul insists that grace and works cannot be mixed: But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace (Rom 11:6). Grace plus anything is no longer grace.

And grace is given to the undeserving. It is not God's favour to good people, or even to people who are trying. It is favour to the ungodly. Paul speaks of God as the one who justifies the ungodly (Rom 4:5). but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8). Grace does not find us worthy. It makes us accepted.

Most of all, grace is personal. It is not a substance God pours into us or a force in the universe. It is God himself, turning toward us in kindness, and it comes to us in a person. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace (John 1:16). To receive grace is to receive Christ.
1.theology:
Grace and mercy: The two are closely linked and often appear together. Mercy is God's compassion toward the miserable and guilty, withholding the punishment they deserve. Grace is his favour toward the undeserving, giving the blessing they could never earn. In Christ we receive both.

Grace is costly to God: Grace is free to us, but it was not cheap. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Cor 8:9). Every gift of grace was purchased by the Son of God.

Grace before time: God's grace did not begin when we believed. He saved us because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began (2 Tim 1:9). Grace goes back to eternity.

Grace for God's glory: God saves by grace to the praise of his glorious grace (Eph 1:6). If we contributed to our salvation, we would share the glory. Because salvation is all of grace, all the glory goes to God, and that is our deepest joy too.
1.examples:
Then: One of the criminals crucified beside Jesus had no time to reform his life, be baptized, attend church or do good works. He simply turned to Jesus and said, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. And Jesus answered, Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:42-43). He is the clearest picture in the Gospels of salvation by grace alone.

Now: A man raised in church has quietly believed for years that God accepts him because he is a decent person: he attends, gives, and avoids the obvious sins. When he finally understands Ephesians 2, it is both humbling and liberating. Humbling, because his goodness counts for nothing in his salvation. Liberating, because he no longer has to keep up the performance. For the first time he rests.

A simple test: Finish this sentence honestly: "God accepts me because..." If anything after "because" is about you, your faithfulness, your effort or your goodness, you have not yet fully grasped grace. The only true answer is, "because of Jesus Christ."

verseByVerse.quote: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul uses three ways to say the same thing. Salvation is by grace, it is not your own doing, and it is not a result of works. Faith is the hand that receives the gift, not a work that earns it. And the purpose is stated plainly: so that no one may boast. In heaven no one will say, "I made the right choice," or "I was more spiritual than others." Everyone will say, "It was all grace." That is why grace humbles us and fills us with joy at the same time.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse is a logical knife. If salvation is by grace, then it cannot be by works, even partly. Grace with a little bit of works is like a gift with a small invoice attached; it is no longer a gift. Many people believe God helps those who help themselves, or that grace makes up the difference after we have done our best. Paul will have none of it. Otherwise grace would no longer be grace. Either grace saves completely, or it does not save at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. (John bore witness about him, and cried out, "This was he of whom I said, 'He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me.'") For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John describes the coming of Jesus in terms of grace. He was full of grace and truth. From his fullness we receive grace upon grace, one gift piled on another, wave after wave without end. And then John compares Moses and Christ: the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. The law was good, but it could only show us God's standard. Christ brings what the law could never give: grace that forgives and transforms. Grace does not come to us as an idea. It comes as a person.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul contrasts two people. One works and receives wages, which are his due. The other does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly. The phrase is astonishing. God justifies, declares righteous, the ungodly. Not the nearly good or the improving, but the ungodly. This is the heart of the gospel. Our faith rests not on our performance but on a God who delights to save those who cannot save themselves. And Paul shows that this was always God's way: Abraham himself was justified by faith (Rom 4:3).

1.reflection:
How would you explain the difference between grace and mercy to a child?

Why do you think the human heart resists the idea of grace so strongly?

Read Ephesians 2:1-10. Which phrase about grace strikes you most, and why?

Finish the sentence: "God accepts me because..." What does your answer reveal?

2.title: The God of All Grace in the Old Testament
2.overview:
Some people imagine that the Old Testament shows a God of law and wrath, and the New Testament a God of grace and love. But the God of the Old Testament describes himself first of all as gracious. When Moses asked to see God's glory, The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (Exod 34:6). This self-description is quoted again and again throughout the Old Testament (for example Neh 9:17; Ps 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2).

Grace runs through the Old Testament story from the beginning. After the fall, God came looking for Adam and Eve, clothed them and promised a Savior (Gen 3:15, 21). In a world so corrupt that God resolved to judge it, Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD (Gen 6:8). God chose Abraham, from a family that served other gods (Josh 24:2), and made promises to him. He chose Jacob, a deceiver. And he chose Israel, not because they were impressive: It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you (Deut 7:7-8).

Even the law was given in grace. Before the Ten Commandments, God said, I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (Exod 20:2). Redemption came first, then the law. Israel did not keep the law in order to be saved; they were given the law because they had been saved.

And when Israel failed again and again, God's grace persisted. The prophets are full of tender invitations: let him return to the LORD, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon (Isa 55:7). Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression? (Mic 7:18). The God of the Old Testament is the God of all grace.
2.theology:
One God, one way of salvation: God has never saved anyone by works. Old Testament believers were saved by grace through faith, looking forward to God's promised redemption, just as we look back to it. Paul uses Abraham and David as his examples of justification by faith (Rom 4:1-8).

Grace and justice together: In Exodus 34 God is gracious, but who will by no means clear the guilty (Exod 34:7). His grace never sets aside his justice. The Old Testament leaves a question hanging: how can God forgive sin and still not clear the guilty? The sacrifices pointed toward the answer, and the cross supplied it.

Grace is God's choice: God's love for Israel was not caused by anything in Israel. the LORD loves you because he loves you (Deut 7:8). That sounds circular, but it is the deepest comfort. A love that is not caused by our goodness cannot be lost by our failure.

New every morning: Even in the ruins of Jerusalem, Jeremiah could write, The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning (Lam 3:22-23). Grace is not a single event but a daily supply.
2.examples:
Then: After King Saul's death, David asked, Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show the kindness of God to him? (2 Sam 9:3). The answer was Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, lame in both feet, living in obscurity and probably afraid that the new king would kill him as a rival. Instead David restored his land and said, you shall eat at my table always (2 Sam 9:7). Mephibosheth had nothing to offer; he was welcomed for another's sake. That is grace: we are welcomed to the King's table for the sake of Christ.

Then: Jonah ran from God precisely because he knew God was gracious. He did not want Nineveh forgiven: for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful (Jonah 4:2). Sometimes we resent God's grace to others even while we depend on it ourselves.

Now: A woman reading the Old Testament for the first time expects to find a harsh God. Instead she finds the God who clothes Adam and Eve, who hears Hagar in the desert (Gen 16:13), who forgives David, who pleads with Israel through the prophets. She realizes that the God of grace was there all along, and that Jesus is not a different God but the fullest revelation of the same one.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children and the children's children, to the third and the fourth generation." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is God's own description of himself, given to Moses just after Israel's sin with the golden calf. God had every reason to destroy them. Instead he proclaimed his name: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness. Notice that grace comes first and dominates the description. But God also says he will by no means clear the guilty. Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter. The tension is resolved only at the cross, where God forgives the guilty by bearing their guilt himself.

verseByVerse.quote: It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the LORD set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the LORD loves you and is keeping the oath that he swore to your fathers, that the LORD has brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel might have assumed that God chose them because they were special. Moses says the opposite. They were the fewest of all peoples. The only reason given for God's love is God's love: because the LORD loves you. This is the pattern of grace in every age. God does not choose people because they are impressive. He chooses them, and then makes them something. Paul says the same of the Corinthian church: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards (1 Cor 1:26).

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to him, "Do not fear, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat at my table always." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Mephibosheth came before David expecting death, and David said, Do not fear. He restored everything Saul had lost and gave Mephibosheth a permanent place at the king's table, for the sake of your father Jonathan. The chapter ends by reminding us that Mephibosheth was lame in both his feet (2 Sam 9:13). He never became impressive. He simply ate at the king's table for the rest of his life. That is a picture of every believer: still weak, still dependent, and always welcome for Christ's sake.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of his inheritance? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love. He will again have compassion on us; he will tread our iniquities underfoot. You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Micah ends his prophecy with a question that is also a play on his own name, which asks, "Who is like the LORD?" His answer: no other God pardons like this. God delights in steadfast love. He does not forgive reluctantly. And the images are vivid: he treads our iniquities underfoot, and You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea. Sins thrown into the deepest sea are gone for good. Grace does not keep a record, waiting to bring them up again.

2.reflection:
Have you ever thought of the Old Testament God as harsh? How does Exodus 34:6-7 challenge that idea?

Read 2 Samuel 9. In what ways are you like Mephibosheth?

Why is it a comfort that God's love for his people is not caused by anything in them (Deut 7:7-8)?

Like Jonah, do you ever resent God's grace to others? Why?

3.title: Saving Grace
3.overview:
How does a person come to be saved? Ephesians 2 answers by describing what we were before grace. And you were dead in the trespasses and sins (Eph 2:1). Not sick, not struggling, but dead. Spiritually dead people cannot make themselves alive. Then come two of the most wonderful words in the Bible: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ— by grace you have been saved (Eph 2:4-5).

Saving grace has many parts, and Scripture shows them as a chain. God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Eph 1:4). He sent his Son to redeem them. By his Spirit he calls them, opening their hearts to believe. He justifies them, declaring them righteous for Christ's sake. He adopts them, sanctifies them and will glorify them. And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified (Rom 8:30). Every link is God's work.

Even faith itself is a gift. Jesus said, No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). When Paul preached at Philippi, The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul (Acts 16:14). Lydia believed because God opened her heart. Faith is truly ours, but it is born of God's grace.

This does not make evangelism pointless or human response unreal. God uses the preaching of the gospel to call his people, and everyone who comes to Christ is welcomed: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). The invitation is genuine and goes to everyone. But when anyone comes, the credit goes to God, not to the sinner.
3.theology:
Can saving grace be resisted? Christians answer this in two main ways. The Arminian view holds that God gives grace to all people, enabling them to believe, but that each person decides whether to accept or resist it. The Reformed view holds that God's saving call to his chosen people is effectual: by his Spirit he gives them a new heart so that they willingly come. Both views agree that people are responsible for their unbelief and that the gospel offer is genuine. The Reformed view is the more likely reading of Scripture. People dead in sin need resurrection, not assistance (Eph 2:5); All that the Father gives me will come to me (John 6:37); and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed (Acts 13:48). God does not drag anyone unwilling into his kingdom. He makes the unwilling willing, and so the saved have nothing to boast of.

Justified by grace: Believers are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Rom 3:24). Justification is God's legal declaration that we are righteous in his sight, based not on our righteousness but on Christ's, received by faith.

Kept by grace: The grace that saves also keeps. he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:6). True believers will persevere, not because they are strong, but because God's grace holds them.

Regeneration: God saved us by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit (Titus 3:5). The new birth is the beginning of the Christian life, and it is entirely God's work.
3.examples:
Then: Saul of Tarsus was on his way to arrest Christians when the risen Christ stopped him on the Damascus road. He was not seeking God; he was fighting him. Later he wrote, formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy (1 Tim 1:13). And he saw his own conversion as a pattern: Christ saved him as an example to those who were to believe in him (1 Tim 1:16). If grace could save Saul, it can save anyone.

Then: Zacchaeus climbed a tree out of curiosity. Jesus stopped, called him by name and invited himself to his house. By the end of the day Zacchaeus was giving away his wealth, and Jesus said, For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). Zacchaeus thought he was looking for Jesus. Jesus was looking for him.

Now: A Christian who prayed for her brother for twenty years wonders whether it was worth it. Then he comes to faith, and he tells her he cannot explain it: he had heard the gospel many times, but one day it suddenly made sense, and he could not resist it. She realizes that her prayers were not wasted. God was at work all along, and his grace was the decisive cause.

verseByVerse.quote: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ— by grace you have been saved— and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: But God. After three verses of devastating description, everything turns on those two words. God acts out of his own character: rich in mercy, moved by the great love with which he loved us. He acted even when we were dead. He made us alive, raised us up and seated us with Christ. And the purpose stretches into eternity: so that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace. Our salvation will be a display of grace forever. Heaven will never run out of reasons to praise it.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This passage gathers the whole gospel into a few lines. God's goodness and loving kindness appeared. He saved us not because of works done by us in righteousness, even our best deeds, but according to his own mercy. He did it through the new birth by the Holy Spirit, poured out richly. And the result is that being justified by his grace we might become heirs. Every part of salvation is from God, and the end is an inheritance we could never earn.

verseByVerse.quote: All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse holds together two truths that people often separate. All that the Father gives me will come to me: God's grace is effective, and those he has given to the Son will certainly come. And whoever comes to me I will never cast out: the invitation is open, and no one who comes will be turned away. The first truth gives assurance that God's purposes cannot fail. The second gives every sinner a reason to come. No one who comes to Christ need wonder whether they are chosen. Their coming is the evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Lydia was a successful businesswoman and a worshipper of God. She heard Paul preach by the river. Luke tells us exactly why she believed: The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. Paul preached; Lydia listened; but the Lord opened her heart. That is how conversion always works. The preacher speaks to the ear, but only God can open the heart. That is why prayer must always accompany evangelism.

3.reflection:
Read Ephesians 2:1-10. What does it mean that we were "dead" in sin, and why does that matter for understanding grace?

How does knowing that God opens hearts (Acts 16:14) affect the way you pray for and speak to unbelievers?

How does John 6:37 hold together God's sovereignty and the open invitation of the gospel?

Paul saw his conversion as an example (1 Tim 1:16). Whose conversion are you praying for?

4.title: Grace Against Legalism and Licence
4.overview:
Grace has two great enemies, and they come from opposite directions.

The first is legalism. Legalism says that we must earn God's acceptance, or keep it, by our performance. It can look very religious. In Galatia, false teachers taught that believing in Christ was good, but that Gentile converts also needed circumcision and the law of Moses to be truly accepted. Paul's response was fierce: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose (Gal 2:21). To add anything to Christ is to say his death was not enough. You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace (Gal 5:4).

Legalism today rarely looks like circumcision. It looks like believing God loves you more when you have had a good week of devotions; feeling that your standing with God depends on your spiritual performance; adding rules to Scripture and judging others by them; or never being able to rest in forgiveness.

The second enemy is licence. Licence says that since we are saved by grace, it does not matter how we live. Paul anticipated the objection: Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it? (Rom 6:1-2). Jude warned of people who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality (Jude 4). Grace that leaves people comfortable in their sin is not the grace of God.

The answer to both errors is the same: a true understanding of grace. Grace saves us completely apart from works, which destroys legalism. And grace transforms us, which destroys licence. For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age (Titus 2:11-12). Grace is not only a pardon. It is a teacher.
4.theology:
Not under law but under grace: For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace (Rom 6:14). Notice what Paul says this means. Being under grace does not give sin more room; it breaks sin's dominion. The law could command but could not change the heart. Grace changes the heart.

Grace and good works: Ephesians 2 says we are saved not a result of works (Eph 2:9), and then at once that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Eph 2:10). Good works are not the root of salvation but its fruit. We do not work to be saved; we are saved to work.

The law's place: The moral law of God still shows believers how to love God and neighbour. What changes is our relationship to it. It is no longer a ladder to climb to earn acceptance, but a guide for grateful children who are already accepted.

Strengthened by grace: it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods (Heb 13:9). External rules and rituals cannot change the heart. Only grace can.
4.examples:
Then: In Jesus' parable, the prodigal son wasted everything, came home and was embraced by his father before he could finish his speech (Luke 15:20-24). But the elder brother refused to join the celebration. He had worked hard and obeyed, and he resented grace given to the undeserving. Both sons were far from the father: one through licence, one through legalism. The father went out to both.

Now, legalism: A conscientious believer feels she must earn her way back into God's favour after she sins. She avoids prayer for a few days as a kind of penance. Grace tells her to run immediately to the throne of grace, because her acceptance rests on Christ, not on her record.

Now, licence: A young man tells himself that his ongoing sexual relationship outside marriage does not matter, because God will forgive him anyway. Grace answers, "By no means!" The grace that forgives also trains us to say no. A person who uses grace as an excuse to keep sinning should ask whether he has really understood it.

Now, in church life: A congregation slowly develops unwritten rules about clothing, schooling, music and entertainment, and those who do not conform are treated as second-class Christians. Grace calls them back to the essentials of Scripture and to charity on matters where God has not spoken.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul draws out the logic of legalism to its terrible conclusion. If we could be made right with God by keeping the law, then Christ died for no purpose. Every attempt to add our works to Christ's work implies that the cross was unnecessary or insufficient. Legalism is not a harmless excess of zeal. It nullifies the grace of God. That is why Paul was willing to confront even Peter publicly when he began to drift from it (Gal 2:11-14).

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul has just said that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Rom 5:20). Someone might conclude: then let us sin more, so that grace can abound more. Paul's answer is the strongest negative he has: By no means! And his reason is not merely that sin is wrong, but that it no longer fits who we are. How can we who died to sin still live in it? Believers have been united to Christ in his death and resurrection. Living in sin is like a free man going back to his prison cell.

verseByVerse.quote: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Grace has appeared in Jesus Christ, and Paul says it does something surprising: it trains us. Grace is a teacher. It teaches us to say no to ungodliness and yes to godly living. It points us forward to our blessed hope, Christ's return. And it reminds us why Christ died: to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. Grace does not make people lazy. It makes them zealous.

verseByVerse.quote: For certain people have crept in unnoticed who long ago were designated for this condemnation, ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jude warns of a danger inside the church, not outside. Certain people had crept in unnoticed, and their error was to pervert the grace of our God into sensuality. They turned grace into an excuse for immorality. This error is still common: "God is love, so he won't mind." But Jude says that such people deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. Grace that refuses Christ's lordship is not grace at all. True grace leads to a life under his rule.

4.reflection:
Are you more prone to legalism or to licence? How do you see it in your life?

Read Luke 15:11-32. Which son do you identify with more, and what does the father's response teach you?

Why does Paul say that being "under grace" breaks the dominion of sin (Rom 6:14)?

Are there unwritten rules in your church or family that function like legalism? How should grace shape them?

5.title: Grace for Every Day
5.overview:
Grace is not only how the Christian life begins. It is how the Christian life continues. Every day believers live by grace, and God supplies it freely.

Grace for weakness. Paul begged God three times to remove a painful thorn in his flesh (2 Cor 12:7-8). God's answer was not removal but grace: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor 12:9). Paul learned that his weakness was the place where Christ's power was most clearly seen.

Grace for need. Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (Heb 4:16). God's throne is a throne of grace. We can come to it in every trouble, temptation and failure.

Grace for service. Paul said, But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me (1 Cor 15:10). Grace does not make us passive. It powers our work, and it takes the credit.

Grace for suffering. And after you have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you (1 Pet 5:10). He is the God of all grace, enough for every kind of trouble.

Grace for the humble. But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble." (Jas 4:6). Grace flows downhill, to the low places. The proud cannot receive it because they do not think they need it.

And there is a wider grace that God shows to all people, believers and unbelievers alike. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust (Matt 5:45). Every good thing in human life, food, friendship, beauty, art, science, family, is a gift of this common grace.
5.theology:
Common and saving grace: Reformed theology distinguishes common grace, God's goodness to all people that restrains evil and gives every good gift, from saving grace, given to his people in Christ. Common grace explains why unbelievers can be kind, wise and skilled. It also leaves everyone without excuse for not thanking God (Acts 14:17; Rom 1:21).

Grace abounds: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work (2 Cor 9:8). Notice the "all"s: all grace, all sufficiency, all things, all times, every good work. God's grace is never in short supply.

The means of grace: God ordinarily gives his grace through his word, prayer, baptism and the Lord's Supper, and the fellowship of his church. These are not magic, and they do not save by themselves. But they are the channels through which God has promised to strengthen his people.

Grace and contentment: He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom 8:32). If God gave his Son, he will not withhold anything we truly need.
5.examples:
Then: Paul's thorn in the flesh was never removed. But he learned to say, For when I am weak, then I am strong (2 Cor 12:10). Whatever the thorn was, it became a daily reminder of his dependence on Christ.

Now: A mother of a disabled child prays for years for healing that does not come. She feels guilty for being tired and angry. One day she reads 2 Corinthians 12 and realizes that God's answer to her may be the same as his answer to Paul: not removal, but grace sufficient for each day. Her weakness has not disqualified her. It is where Christ's power rests.

Now: A pastor who has served faithfully for decades is asked what kept him going. He answers that every Sunday he felt inadequate, and every Sunday God gave enough grace. "I have never had grace for next week," he says, "only for this week."

Now: A Christian enjoys a sunset, a meal with friends and a beautiful piece of music written by an unbeliever. She thanks God for all of it. Common grace teaches her to see God's kindness everywhere.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to me, "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God's answer to Paul's prayer was "no" to the request and "yes" to something better. My grace is sufficient for you. Not "will be" but "is": the grace is present now. And its purpose: my power is made perfect in weakness. God is not glorified mainly when strong people do impressive things. He is glorified when weak people are held up by his strength. Paul's response is remarkable: he will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses. Grace changes our relationship to our own limitations.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The throne of God was once the place sinners feared most. Now, because Jesus is our great high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses (Heb 4:15), it has become the throne of grace. And we are invited to come with confidence, not because we are worthy but because he is. We come that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need. Mercy for our failures, grace for our struggles. There is no time of need for which this throne is closed.

verseByVerse.quote: But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul knew he did not deserve to be an apostle, having persecuted the church (1 Cor 15:9). So he says, by the grace of God I am what I am. Everything he had become was a gift. But grace did not make him lazy: I worked harder than any of them. And then he corrects himself: though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. This is the paradox of Christian effort. We work hard, and grace gets the credit, because grace was working through our work.

verseByVerse.quote: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, "God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James writes to Christians who are quarrelling, envious and worldly. They are in serious trouble. And yet his first word is hope: But he gives more grace. There is always more grace. Then he quotes Proverbs: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. The condition for receiving more grace is not to become better first, but to become humble: to admit our need and come to God. Pride is the only thing that blocks the flow of grace.

5.reflection:
Where do you most need to hear "My grace is sufficient for you" right now?

How does coming to "the throne of grace" (Heb 4:16) differ from how you usually approach God in prayer?

What does 1 Corinthians 15:10 teach about the relationship between grace and hard work?

Where can you see God's common grace around you this week? Take time to thank him for it.

6.title: Growing in Grace and Showing Grace
6.overview:
Peter's last words in his last letter are a command: But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ (2 Pet 3:18). We never outgrow grace. We grow into it, understanding it more deeply, depending on it more fully and being shaped by it more completely.

We grow in grace through the same means God uses to give it: by reading and hearing his word, which Paul calls the word of his grace, which is able to build you up (Acts 20:32); by prayer at the throne of grace; by the sacraments; and by the fellowship of other believers who remind us of the gospel. Growing in grace also means growing in humility, since grace is given to the humble.

And those who receive grace become people who show it. Grace received must become grace given.

Grace in our words. Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear (Eph 4:29). Our words can be channels of God's grace to others. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6).

Grace in forgiveness. Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Eph 4:32). People who know how much they have been forgiven become forgivers.

Grace in giving. Paul calls the Macedonians' generosity the grace of God at work in them (2 Cor 8:1). He grounds Christian giving in the grace of Christ, who became poor for our sake (2 Cor 8:9).

Grace in service. As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace (1 Pet 4:10). Every gift we have is grace entrusted to us for the good of others.
6.theology:
Grace is the motive: The New Testament does not ground Christian behaviour in guilt or fear of losing God's love. It grounds it in grace already received. We forgive because we were forgiven, give because Christ gave, and serve because we have been served.

Grace is for sharing: The gospel is called the gospel of the grace of God (Acts 20:24). Paul counted his life worth nothing compared with testifying to it. Every believer who has received grace is called to make it known.

Do not receive grace in vain: Paul appealed to the Corinthians not to receive the grace of God in vain (2 Cor 6:1). Grace is meant to bear fruit. A believer who receives grace but never shows it has not yet understood what he has received.

Grace to the end: Paul's letters almost always begin and end with grace. Christian life starts in grace, continues in grace and ends in glory, where we will spend eternity discovering the immeasurable riches of his grace (Eph 2:7).
6.examples:
Then: When Barnabas visited the new church in Antioch, Luke says, When he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad (Acts 11:23). Grace is visible. Barnabas could see it in the changed lives of the believers there, and it made him rejoice.

Now, in words: A man known for his sharp tongue begins to pray Ephesians 4:29 every morning. He starts noticing how often his words tear down. Slowly, by grace, he learns to encourage his wife, praise his children and speak kindly to difficult colleagues. People begin to say he has mellowed. He knows it is grace.

Now, in forgiveness: A woman whose husband betrayed her years ago finds she still carries bitterness. She reads Hebrews 12:15, See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no "root of bitterness" springs up. She realizes that forgiving does not mean pretending nothing happened, but releasing the debt as God released hers. It takes time, and grace.

Now, in giving: A couple on a modest income decide to support a missionary family. They cannot give much, but they give gladly. They are learning the grace of giving.

This week: Read Ephesians 2 and Titus 3 slowly. Thank God for one specific grace each day. Forgive someone, speak a gracious word to someone and give something away, as a response to grace.

verseByVerse.quote: But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter's final instruction is not a new rule or a complex doctrine. It is a call to growth: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Grace and knowledge belong together. As we know Christ better, we understand his grace more deeply, and as we experience his grace, we know him more truly. And Peter ends with praise: To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Growth in grace always leads to glory for Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul says that our words can give grace to those who hear. That is a remarkable thought. The same grace God gives us can flow through our speech to others. Then he names what destroys grace in a community: bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour, slander and malice (Eph 4:31). And he calls us to the opposite: kindness, tenderness and forgiveness, as God in Christ forgave you. The measure of our forgiveness is God's forgiveness of us, and the power for it is his grace in us.

verseByVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul is raising money for poor believers in Jerusalem, and he does not use pressure or guilt. He points to Christ: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. Christ's self-giving is the pattern and power of all Christian generosity. People who have been made rich by Christ's poverty will find it natural to give. Generosity is grace flowing outward.

verseByVerse.quote: As each has received a gift, use it to serve one another, as good stewards of God's varied grace: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Every believer has received some gift: teaching, serving, encouraging, giving, leading, showing mercy. Peter calls these gifts God's varied grace, grace in many colours. And he calls us stewards, managers of something that belongs to someone else. Our gifts are not for our own glory but for serving one another. A church where every member uses their gift is a church where the many-coloured grace of God is on display.

6.reflection:
In what ways have you grown in your understanding of grace over the years?

Read Ephesians 4:25-32. Which instruction about speech or forgiveness do you most need to apply?

Is there someone you need to forgive "as God in Christ forgave you"?

What gift has God entrusted to you, and how could you use it to serve others as a steward of his grace?
